```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE, fig.pos = "htbp")
template_dir <- "../../_shared/template"
source(file.path(template_dir, "viscount_rmd_helpers.R"))
library(jsonlite)

read_json5_clean <- function(path) {
  lines <- readLines(path, warn = FALSE, encoding = "UTF-8")
  text <- paste(lines, collapse = "\n")
  text <- gsub("//[^\n]*", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub("/\\*.*?\\*/", "", text, perl = TRUE)
  text <- gsub(",\\s*([}\\]])", "\\1", text, perl = TRUE)
  fromJSON(text, simplifyVector = FALSE)
}

mod_data <- read_json5_clean("post_soviet_central_asia.json5")
sett_data <- fromJSON("post_soviet_central_asia_settlements.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
ledger_data <- read_json5_clean("post_soviet_central_asia_source_ledger.json5")
diag_data <- fromJSON("../../_shared/sites_saray_central_asia/config/kriging_diagnostics.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
geo_data <- fromJSON("../../_shared/sites_saray_central_asia/config/sites_saray_central_asia_geojson_metadata.json", simplifyVector = FALSE)
```

# Abstract

This paper reconstructs the demographic trajectory, macro-spatial distribution and settlement systems of post-Soviet Central Asia across the thirty-five years spanning the dissolution of the Soviet Union in December 1991 to 2026. Encompassing 3.890.946 km² divided into forty-eight administrative territories across Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan, the aggregate population expanded from 50,95M (50.949.998) in 1991 to 82,67M (82.668.004) by 2025, marking an overall demographic increment of 62,3% (+31,72M inhabitants). This aggregate growth conceals two profoundly divergent demographic regimes. In the northern steppe domain of Kazakhstan, the severe economic contraction of the 1990s and massive outward emigration of European minorities depressed population to an intercensal trough before rising titular birth rates, state-assisted repatriation programmes and rapid growth in Astana, Almaty and Shymkent propelled total numbers to 20,22M by 2025 [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment; @Sushchiy2021Russian; @Anon2026Interethni]. Concurrently, the southern irrigated oasis belt experienced sustained natural increase: Uzbekistan added 16,83M people to attain 37,47M, Tajikistan overcame the acute dislocations of the 1992-1997 Civil War to reach 10,44M, Kyrgyzstan expanded to 7,15M and Turkmenistan expanded across desert oases to 7,40M [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Tukumov2024Societal; @OBrien2019Long; @Group2021Demographi]. This synthesis harmonises round censuses from 1989 through the 2020-2022 series with annual vital registration registers across 3.589 catalogued settlements, providing a coherent quantitative benchmark for the regional demographic transition.

# Background

## Geopolitical Dissolution and the Post-Soviet Transition

The dissolution of the Soviet Union in late 1991 transformed the demographic landscape of Central Asia by converting internal republican boundaries into international frontiers and rupturing the integrated economic mechanisms of the Soviet state [@Nikolaeva2024Changes; @Anon2021Main]. Under late Soviet central planning, regional demography had been monitored through centralised all-Union censuses, notably the benchmark censuses of 1959, 1970, 1979 and 1989 [@Anon2021Transforma; @Zhumashev2024Foreign]. These enumerations captured a region characterized by rapid demographic expansion in the southern Muslim republics alongside large Slavic and European minority populations in northern Kazakhstan and major industrial cities [@Anon2021Transforma; @Sushchiy2021Russian].

With independence, the newly sovereign statistical agencies faced the formidable challenge of establishing autonomous demographic registers amid hyperinflation, administrative restructuring and the termination of direct fiscal subsidies from Moscow [@Kurbanova2022Impact; @Petrick2021Post]. The immediate post-independence decade was marked by severe economic dislocation [@Kurbanova2022Impact; @Tukumov2024Societal]. Industrial enterprises lost traditional supply chains, collective state farms (*kolkhozy* and *sovkhozy*) were restructured or dismantled and public healthcare and family allowance systems experienced acute financial shortfalls [@Petrick2021Post; @Makhanov2025Post].

These socioeconomic shocks exerted divergent demographic pressures across the region. In Kazakhstan and northern Kyrgyzstan, economic stress combined with sociopolitical uncertainty triggered steep reductions in total fertility rates and unprecedented levels of outward emigration [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Sushchiy2021Russian; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. Conversely, in the southern agrarian basins of Uzbekistan and Tajikistan, traditional family structures, high marital propensities and younger age pyramids maintained robust rates of natural increase despite falling real household incomes [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Tukumov2024Societal].

## Divergent Demographic Trajectories Across the Five Republics

The demographic evolution of post-Soviet Central Asia is characterized by stark structural divergence between the steppe north and the oasis south [@Nikolaeva2024Changes; @Tukumov2024Societal]. In Kazakhstan, the 1990s constituted a demographic climacteric [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Makhanov2025Post]. The 1989 Soviet census had recorded 16,46M inhabitants in the Kazakh Soviet Socialist Republic, with ethnic Kazakhs constituting a minority (39,7%) within their own republic alongside large Russian (37,8%), German (5,8%) and Ukrainian (5,4%) populations [@Anon2021Transforma; @Sushchiy2021Russian]. Outward migration during the 1990s exceeded two million people, pulling the national headcount down to 14,95M in the 1999 census [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment]. Only after 2000 did petroleum-led economic recovery, rising marital fertility and substantial state incentives for ethnic Kazakh repatriation reverse this trajectory, lifting the population through 16,01M in 2009 and 19,19M in 2021 to 20,22M by 2025 [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Anon2026Interethni].

Uzbekistan followed an uninterrupted upward trajectory [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Kurbanova2022Impact]. Standing at 20,64M in 1991, the republic expanded by an average of 495k people per year over thirty-four years, reaching 37,47M in 2025 [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Group2021Demographi]. High fertility in the dense agricultural heartlands of the Fergana Valley, Samarkand and Qashqadaryo sustained substantial annual natural increments that routinely offset outward labour migration [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. By 2025, Uzbekistan accounted for 45,3% of the total population of Central Asia, confirming its position as the demographic core of the region [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Tukumov2024Societal].

Tajikistan experienced the most violent disruption of the post-Soviet transition [@OBrien2019Long; @Hameed2023Analyzing]. The outbreak of the Tajik Civil War (1992-1997) resulted in an estimated 50k to 100k fatalities and the displacement of over 600k citizens, including tens of thousands of refugees who crossed into northern Afghanistan [@OBrien2019Long; @Hameed2023Analyzing]. Despite war-related excess mortality and displacement, underlying natural increase remained exceptionally high [@OBrien2019Long; @Tukumov2024Societal]. Following the 1997 peace accord, population growth rebounded rapidly: the republic expanded from 5,26M in 1991 to 6,13M in the 2000 census, 7,56M in 2010 and reached 10,44M by 2025 [@OBrien2019Long; @Kurbanova2024Demographi].

Kyrgyzstan navigated a dual demographic regime [@Somerlikova2025Causes; @Group2021Demographi]. The northern oblasts of Chuy and Issyk-Kul, together with the capital Bishkek, recorded substantial outward Russian and Slavic migration, whereas the southern oblasts of Osh, Jalal-Abad and Batken in the Fergana basin maintained high birth rates [@Somerlikova2025Causes; @Group2021Demographi]. The national population expanded from 4,35M in 1991 to 4,82M in the 1999 census, 5,36M in 2009, 6,75M in 2022 and reached 7,15M by 2025 [@Group2021Demographi; @Tukumov2024Societal].

Turkmenistan expanded from 3,79M in 1991 to 7,40M in 2025 under centralized administrative governance [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main]. While official censuses in 1995, 2012 and 2022 reported sustained demographic growth, independent demographic observers have noted methodological discrepancies regarding international emigration and vital registration completeness [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main]. The regional figures harmonised in this study capture the documented spatial distribution of habitation across the five velayats and the expanding urban core of Ashgabat [@Group2021Demographi].

## Migration Dynamics, Slavic Emigration and Rural-to-Urban Mobility

International migration represented the single most powerful demographic redistribution mechanism across Central Asia during the initial post-Soviet decades [@Sushchiy2021Russian; @Massey2023Shape; @Lerpold2023Migration]. The primary migration stream comprised the repatriation of non-titular European populations toward the Russian Federation, Germany, Ukraine and Belarus [@Sushchiy2021Russian; @Nikolaeva2024Changes; @Anon2021Main]. Between 1989 and 2005, over 1,5M ethnic Russians, 600k Germans and hundreds of thousands of Ukrainians and Tatars emigrated from Kazakhstan alone [@Sushchiy2021Russian; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment; @Miazin2025Developmen]. Similar proportional outflows affected northern Kyrgyzstan, the mining towns of Tajikistan and major industrial centres in Uzbekistan [@Sushchiy2021Russian; @OBrien2019Long].

This outward Slavic migration fundamentally altered the ethnic balance across the region [@Nikolaeva2024Changes; @Anon2021Main]. The proportion of titular nationalities surged: ethnic Kazakhs increased from 39,7% in 1989 to 70,4% by 2021; Uzbeks expanded from 71,4% to over 84% in Uzbekistan; and Kyrgyz, Tajiks and Turkmens came to constitute over 75% to 85% of their respective national populations [@Nikolaeva2024Changes; @Anon2026Interethni; @Anon2021Main]. In Kazakhstan, this process was deliberately accelerated through the *oralman* (subsequently termed *qandas*) repatriation programme, which resettled over one million ethnic Kazakhs from China, Mongolia, Uzbekistan, Russia and Iran into northern and urban regions [@Anon2026Interethni; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment].

From the late 1990s onward, international labour migration emerged as an indispensable socioeconomic safety valve [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes; @Golunov2025Central]. Hundreds of thousands of young adult males from rural Tajikistan, southern Kyrgyzstan and rural Uzbekistan migrated seasonally or semi-permanently to Russian construction, manufacturing and service sectors [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. At its peak, remittances contributed between 25% and 45% of gross domestic product in Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan, supporting rural household consumption while creating pronounced imbalances in working-age sex ratios in origin settlements [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes; @Kurbanova2022Impact].

Concurrently, internal rural-to-urban migration reshaped domestic settlement geographies [@Makhanov2025Post; @Aubakirova2024Regional; @Cividino2020Revisiting]. The closure of unprofitable Soviet collective farms and the downsizing of northern industrial single-industry towns (*monogoroda*) drove substantial population movements toward primary metropolitan centres [@Makhanov2025Post; @Aubakirova2024Regional]. In Kazakhstan, internal migrants flowed steadily from the declining agricultural settlements of Kostanay, North Kazakhstan and East Kazakhstan toward Almaty, Astana and Shymkent [@Makhanov2025Post; @Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment]. In Kyrgyzstan, internal movement from Naryn and the southern mountains concentrated into the sprawling peri-urban settlements (*novostroiki*) ringing Bishkek and Osh [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting].

## Contemporary Urbanisation and Metropolisation

The urban hierarchy of post-Soviet Central Asia underwent profound restructuring [@Cividino2020Revisiting; @Group2021Demographi]. Tashkent consolidated its role as the undisputed primate city of the region, expanding from 2,13M in 1991 to 3,11M by 2025 (metro exceeding 3,5M), anchoring modern transport, commercial and educational networks [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting].

In Kazakhstan, the relocation of the national capital from Almaty to Akmola (renamed Astana, later Nur-Sultan and restored to Astana) in December 1997 constituted one of the most ambitious state-directed urban projects in modern Eurasia [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment]. Astana expanded from a provincial steppe railway town of 303k in 1991 to 1,40M in its administrative core and 1,64M in its broader agglomeration by 2025 [@Aubakirova2024Regional]. Despite losing political capital status, Almaty retained its pre-eminence as Kazakhstan's commercial and financial centre, doubling from 1,16M in 1991 to 2,30M (metro 2,35M) in 2025 [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment]. In 2018, Shymkent achieved city of republican significance status after surpassing one million inhabitants, establishing a dynamic tri-polar urban structure in Kazakhstan [@Aubakirova2024Regional].

Bishkek in Kyrgyzstan expanded from 658k in 1991 to 1,15M (metro 1,36M) in 2025, while Dushanbe in Tajikistan doubled from 607k to 1,23M (metro 1,29M), reflecting intense demographic centralization in national capitals [@Group2021Demographi; @OBrien2019Long]. In Turkmenistan, Ashgabat underwent comprehensive state-funded urban transformation, expanding from 450k to 1,07M across expansive planned boulevards [@Group2021Demographi]. Alongside these national capitals, dense secondary urban networks in the Fergana Valley (Namangan 713k, Andijan 548k, Fergana 328k) and ancient Silk Road oases (Samarkand 596k, Bukhara 280k) maintained vital regional commercial and manufacturing roles [@Group2021Demographi; @Kurbanova2024Demographi].

# Methodology

## Administrative Structure and Territorial Partition

To evaluate the demographic transformation of post-Soviet Central Asia with spatial fidelity, this study partitions the domain into forty-eight administrative territories across five sovereign republics, encompassing 3.890.946 km² across 65.332 five-arcminute grid cells (Table \ref{tab:validation-post-soviet}):

1. Kazakhstan (16 territories, 2.715.352 km²): Three cities of republican significance (Almaty City, Astana City and Shymkent included within Turkistan Oblast) alongside fourteen oblasts (Almaty, Akmola, Aktobe, Atyrau, East Kazakhstan, Mangystau, North Kazakhstan, Pavlodar, Karaganda, Kostanay, Kyzylorda, Turkistan (South Kazakhstan), West Kazakhstan and Jambyl).
2. Uzbekistan (14 territories, 447.387 km²): Tashkent City, Tashkent Region, the Republic of Karakalpakstan and eleven regions (Andijan, Bukhara, Fergana, Jizzakh, Qashqadaryo, Xorazm, Namangan, Navoiy, Samarkand, Sirdaryo and Surxondaryo).
3. Tajikistan (5 territories, 135.246 km²): Dushanbe City, Gorno-Badakhshan Autonomous Region, Khatlon Region, Sughd (Leninabad) Region and Districts of Republican Subordination.
4. Kyrgyzstan (8 territories, 193.291 km²): Bishkek City, Chuy Region, Batken, Jalal-Abad, Naryn, Osh Region and City, Talas and Issyk-Kul.
5. Turkmenistan (5 territories, 492.130 km²): Ahal Region with Ashgabat, Balkan, Lebap, Mary and Dashoguz.

At each five-year benchmark year $t \in \{1991, 1995, 2000, 2005, 2010, 2015, 2020, 2025\}$, total regional population $P_r(t)$ synthesises official census round counts, annual vital registration statistics and administrative registers:

$$P_r(t) = C_r(t) + \sum_{y=t_{\text{census}}}^{t} \left( B_r(y) - D_r(y) + M_r^{\text{net}}(y) \right) + \delta_r(t)$$

where $C_r(t)$ represents the baseline census headcount, $B_r(y)$ and $D_r(y)$ denote registered births and deaths, $M_r^{\text{net}}(y)$ captures net internal and international migration flows and $\delta_r(t)$ represents the intercensal reconciliation adjustment factor calibrated by national statistical bureaus [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment; @Group2021Demographi].

## Multi-Source Census Reconciliation and Vital Registration

Demographic parameters are harmonised from national census publications and annual statistical yearbooks:
- Kazakhstan: 1989 All-Union Census, 1999 First National Census, 2009 National Population Census, 2021 National Population Census and Bureau of National Statistics annual registers [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment; @Anon2026Interethni].
- Uzbekistan: 1989 All-Union Census, Ministry of Economy and Finance demographic updates and Statistics Agency under the President of Uzbekistan annual demographic yearbooks [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Group2021Demographi].
- Tajikistan: 1989 All-Union Census, 2000 First National Census, 2010 National Population Census, 2020 Census of Population and Housing and Agency on Statistics under the President of Tajikistan reports [@OBrien2019Long; @Kurbanova2024Demographi].
- Kyrgyzstan: 1989 All-Union Census, 1999 National Population Census, 2009 Population and Housing Census, 2022 National Population and Housing Census and National Statistical Committee registers [@Group2021Demographi; @Somerlikova2025Causes].
- Turkmenistan: 1989 All-Union Census, 1995 National Census, 2012 Complete Population and Housing Census, 2022 National Census and State Committee of Turkmenistan on Statistics summaries [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main].

## Spatial Distribution and Environmental Covariates

Spatial population allocation across the forty-eight administrative territories draws on the regional kriging domain, integrating 12.473 domestic assigned archaeological and historical records alongside modern settlement coordinates across 442 domestic catchments (covering 65.332 raster cells) [@Mukhamejan2026Long; @Petrick2021Post]. Residual spatial dependence is modelled with non-stationary Matérn ($\nu = 3/2$) kriging:

$$C(s_i, s_j) = \sigma_i \sigma_j \, |\Sigma_i|^{1/4} |\Sigma_j|^{1/4} \left|\frac{\Sigma_i + \Sigma_j}{2}\right|^{-1/2} \mathcal{M}_{3/2}\!\left(\sqrt{Q_{ij}}\right)$$

Regularised dimensionless variogram bandwidths stand at $\tau_1 = 1,50$, with residual $R^2$ consistently exceeding 0,998 across all historical horizons (Table \ref{tab:kriging-saray}). Spatial distribution incorporates five primary covariates: habitable land fraction, fluvial corridor proximity (Amu Darya, Syr Darya, Irtysh, Ili and Chu river systems), irrigation infrastructure density, piedmont terrain suitability and urban buffer distance [@Petrick2021Post; @Golunov2025Central]. High-density settlement cores from 3.589 catalogued settlements condition local density clusters, with urban masks applied to preserve rural demographic baselines [@Cividino2020Revisiting; @Group2021Demographi].

# Testing and Validation

Arithmetic reconciliation confirms exact parity between territorial totals and national aggregates across all five republics. Table \ref{tab:validation-post-soviet} documents the longitudinal demographic trajectory across eight benchmark years from 1991 to 2025, decomposed by sovereign republic.

```{r tab-validation, results='asis'}
benchmarks <- c("1991", "1995", "2000", "2005", "2010", "2015", "2020", "2025")

kz_keys <- grep("^kz_", names(mod_data$regions), value = TRUE)
uz_keys <- grep("^uz_", names(mod_data$regions), value = TRUE)
tj_keys <- grep("^tj_", names(mod_data$regions), value = TRUE)
kg_keys <- grep("^kg_", names(mod_data$regions), value = TRUE)
tm_keys <- grep("^tm_", names(mod_data$regions), value = TRUE)

sum_group <- function(keys, yr) {
  sum(vapply(keys, function(k) as.numeric(mod_data$regions[[k]]$population[[yr]]), numeric(1)))
}

val_rows <- lapply(benchmarks, function(yr) {
  p_kz <- sum_group(kz_keys, yr)
  p_uz <- sum_group(uz_keys, yr)
  p_tj <- sum_group(tj_keys, yr)
  p_kg <- sum_group(kg_keys, yr)
  p_tm <- sum_group(tm_keys, yr)
  p_tot <- p_kz + p_uz + p_tj + p_kg + p_tm
  data.frame(
    Benchmark = yr,
    Kazakhstan = viscount_fmt_pop(p_kz),
    Uzbekistan = viscount_fmt_pop(p_uz),
    Tajikistan = viscount_fmt_pop(p_tj),
    Kyrgyzstan = viscount_fmt_pop(p_kg),
    Turkmenistan = viscount_fmt_pop(p_tm),
    Total = viscount_fmt_pop(p_tot),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
val_df <- do.call(rbind, val_rows)
rownames(val_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  val_df,
  "Macro-regional demographic benchmarks across the five sovereign Central Asian republics, 1991 to 2025, harmonised from national censuses and statistical committees.",
  c("Year", "Kazakhstan", "Uzbekistan", "Tajikistan", "Kyrgyzstan", "Turkmenistan", "Domain Total"),
  list(label = "tab:validation-post-soviet", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

Across the regional kriging domain, Table \ref{tab:kriging-saray} documents tightly constrained Matérn variogram parameters across all nine chronological horizons. Residual $R^2$ exceeds 0,998 across all epochs, demonstrating high spatial stability from prehistoric antiquity through the modern census era.

```{r tab-kriging, results='asis'}
saray_labels <- c(
  `01_epipalaeolithic_mesolithic_early_neolithic` = "1. Epipalaeolithic, Mesolithic and Early Neolithic (before 4000BC)",
  `02_chalcolithic_namazga_sarazm_botai` = "2. Chalcolithic, Namazga, Sarazm and Botai (4000BC to 2500BC)",
  `03_bronze_age_bmac_sintashta_andronovo` = "3. Bronze Age BMAC, Sintashta and Andronovo (2500BC to 1000BC)",
  `04_iron_age_saka_achaemenid_hellenistic` = "4. Iron Age Saka, Achaemenid and Hellenistic (1000BC to 250BC)",
  `05_kushan_kangju_wusun_parthian_antiquity` = "5. Kushan, Kangju, Wusun and Parthian Antiquity (250BC to 500AD)",
  `06_sogdian_turkic_early_islamic` = "6. Sogdian, Early Turkic and Early Islamic (500AD to 900AD)",
  `07_samanid_karakhanid_seljuk_khwarazmshah` = "7. Samanid, Karakhanid, Seljuk and Khwarazmshah (900AD to 1219AD)",
  `08_mongol_chagatai_timurid` = "8. Mongol, Chagatai and Timurid Zenith (1219AD to 1500AD)",
  `09_uzbek_khanates_kazakh_zhuzes` = "9. Uzbek Khanates, Kazakh Zhuzes and Imperial Eras (1500AD to 1917AD)"
)
saray_horizons <- names(diag_data$variogram_models)
krig_df <- data.frame(
  Horizon = unname(saray_labels[saray_horizons]),
  Tau1 = vapply(saray_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$tau1_dimensionless, 2L), character(1)),
  Nugget = vapply(saray_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$c0_nugget, 6L), character(1)),
  Nugget_Sill = vapply(saray_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$nugget_to_sill_ratio, 2L), character(1)),
  Residual_R2 = vapply(saray_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$variogram_models[[h]]$residual_r2, 4L), character(1)),
  Mean_Cell = vapply(saray_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$mean_value, 4L), character(1)),
  P99_Cell = vapply(saray_horizons, function(h) viscount_fmt_number(diag_data$kriged_raster_stats[[h]]$p99_value, 4L), character(1)),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
rownames(krig_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  krig_df,
  "Regional kriging variogram diagnostics across nine chronological horizons (65.332 raster cells, regularised tau1 = 1,50).",
  c("Kriging Horizon", "Tau1", "Nugget c0", "Nugget-to-Sill", "Residual R²", "Mean Cell", "P99 Cell"),
  list(label = "tab:kriging-saray", font_size = "scriptsize")
)
```

Table \ref{tab:source-corpora-saray} details the component archaeological, heritage and administrative corpora aggregated into the regional synthesis, encompassing 41.619 raw records across fourteen primary repositories led by the UCL CAAL database, official national monument registers and peer-reviewed excavation compendia.

```{r tab-source-corpora, results='asis'}
src_labels <- c(
  ucl_caal_dated_horizons = "UCL Central Asian Archaeological Landscape Dated Horizons",
  ucl_caal_typed_monuments = "UCL Central Asian Archaeological Landscape Typed Monuments",
  althurayya_islamic_gazetteer = "Al-Thurayya Classical and Mediaeval Islamic Gazetteer",
  pleiades_antiquity = "Pleiades Classical and Hellenistic Antiquity Gazetteer",
  tegiszhol_c14 = "Tegiszhol and Steppe Bronze Age Radiocarbon Corpus",
  c14bazaar_p3k14c_nerd = "Global Radiocarbon Synthesis (c14bazAAR, p3k14c and NERD)",
  aadr_v66_central_asia_adna = "Allen Ancient DNA Resource Central Asian Compendium (v66)",
  archatlas_2020 = "ArchAtlas Central Asian Archaeological Sites Register",
  uzbekistan_cabinet_res846_register = "Uzbekistan Cabinet of Ministers Resolution No. 846 National Monument Register",
  kazakhstan_adilet_order88_register = "Kazakhstan Ministry of Culture Order No. 88 National Monument Register",
  published_excavations_atlas = "Harvard Dataverse Archaeological Atlas of Published Excavations",
  polaris_ia_ras_frontier = "Institute of Archaeology RAS Steppe Frontier Register",
  jade_xinjiang_frontier = "JADE Central Asian and Tarim Frontier Archaeological Buffer",
  central_asia_scholarly_catalogue = "Central Asian Modern Census and Scholarly Monograph Register"
)

sc_keys <- names(geo_data$source_record_counts)
tot_sc <- sum(as.numeric(unlist(geo_data$source_record_counts)))

sc_rows <- lapply(sc_keys, function(sk) {
  lbl <- if (sk %in% names(src_labels)) unname(src_labels[[sk]]) else sk
  cnt <- as.numeric(geo_data$source_record_counts[[sk]])
  data.frame(
    Registry = lbl,
    Records = viscount_fmt_number(cnt, 0L),
    Share = paste0(viscount_fmt_number(100 * cnt / tot_sc, 2L), "%"),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
sc_df <- do.call(rbind, sc_rows)
rownames(sc_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  sc_df,
  "Component archaeological, heritage and statistical gazetteer registries aggregated into the Central Asian regional domain.",
  c("Source Registry", "Raw Records", "Share"),
  list(label = "tab:source-corpora-saray", font_size = "footnotesize")
)
```

# Results

## Post-Soviet Demographic Expansion and Regional Divergence

Between 1991 and 2025, total population across Central Asia surged from 50,95M to 82,67M, an expansion of 31,72M inhabitants (Figure \ref{fig:traj-post-soviet}). The regional expansion rate accelerated from an initial modest tempo of 1,01% annually during the disrupted 1990s to over 1,55% annually after 2010, driven by the expanding reproductive cohorts of the southern oasis republics [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Tukumov2024Societal].

```{r fig-traj, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig2_post_soviet_central_asia_trajectory.png",
  "Demographic trajectory of post-Soviet Central Asia from 1991 to 2025 across the five sovereign republics with uncertainty intervals.",
  "fig:traj-post-soviet"
)
```

The composition of the regional aggregate shifted decisively toward Uzbekistan and Tajikistan (Table \ref{tab:validation-post-soviet}). In 1991, Uzbekistan accounted for 40,5% of Central Asian inhabitants, Kazakhstan held 33,2%, Tajikistan held 10,3%, Kyrgyzstan sustained 8,5% and Turkmenistan supported 7,4%. By 2025, Uzbekistan's share had risen to 45,3%, while Kazakhstan's share receded to 24,5%. Tajikistan advanced to 12,6%, while Kyrgyzstan and Turkmenistan held 8,6% and 8,9% respectively.

## Kazakhstan: Emigration Trough, Ethnic Rebalancing and Urban Rebound

The demographic evolution of Kazakhstan over the post-Soviet era demonstrates the profound interaction between outward international migration, internal mobility and changing fertility behaviour [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment; @Makhanov2025Post]. In 1991, Kazakhstan sustained 16,90M inhabitants (Table \ref{tab:regions-post-soviet}). Over the subsequent decade, massive emigration of Russian, German, Ukrainian and Belarusian minorities removed over 1,8M net residents, creating an acute demographic contraction in the northern and eastern industrial oblasts [@Sushchiy2021Russian; @Anon2021Main].

North Kazakhstan Oblast contracted from 961k in 1991 to 575k in 2025 (-40,2%), Kostanay contracted from 1,26M to 822k (-35,0%), Pavlodar fell from 961k to 740k (-23,1%), East Kazakhstan declined from 1,82M to 1,31M (-27,8%) and Karaganda shrank from 1,82M to 1,40M (-23,3%) [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Makhanov2025Post]. This widespread depopulation of the northern agricultural and mining belt represented the most severe regional demographic contraction documented in modern Central Asian history [@Makhanov2025Post; @Anon2026].

However, this northern contraction was counterbalanced by dynamic demographic expansion in southern and western Kazakhstan, alongside spectacular growth in the metropolitan centres [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Anon2026Interethni]. Turkistan (South Kazakhstan) Oblast surged from 1,87M in 1991 to 3,37M in 2025 (+80,0%), sustained by the highest natural increase rates in the country and the rapid growth of Shymkent [@Aubakirova2024Regional]. In the western petroleum-producing basins, Mangystau more than doubled from 354k to 822k (+132,0%) and Atyrau expanded from 455k to 740k (+62,4%) [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment].

The most dramatic demographic transformations occurred in the primary urban centres [@Aubakirova2024Regional]. Almaty City doubled from 1,16M in 1991 to 2,30M in 2025, retaining its position as the premier commercial, cultural and higher education hub of Kazakhstan [@Aubakirova2024Regional]. In the north, the designation of Astana as the new national capital triggered rapid immigration of administrative personnel, university students, construction workers and service professionals, expanding the city more than fourfold from 304k in 1991 to 1,40M (1.396.974 in core registers, with metropolitan territory reaching 1,64M) by 2025 [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Zhumashbekova2023Assessment]. By 2025, Kazakhstan's total population stood at 20,22M, having fully overcome the 1990s emigration deficit to establish a fundamentally restructured urbanized nation [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Anon2026Interethni].

## Uzbekistan: The Oasis Demographic Engine and Fergana Densities

Uzbekistan operated as the primary demographic engine of Central Asia throughout the post-Soviet period (Figure \ref{fig:density-post-soviet}) [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Kurbanova2022Impact; @Group2021Demographi]. Expanding from 20,64M in 1991 to 37,47M in 2025, the republic added 16,83M residents without experiencing an intercensal pause (Table \ref{tab:regions-post-soviet}).

```{r fig-density, results='asis'}
viscount_figure(
  "figures/fig3_post_soviet_central_asia_density.png",
  "Population density surface and comparative republic density distributions across Central Asia in 2020.",
  "fig:density-post-soviet"
)
```

This sustained expansion generated extraordinary demographic densities in the irrigated oasis basins, most notably within the Fergana Valley [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Petrick2021Post]. Andijan Region, encompassing a compact territory of 4.340 km², expanded from 1,77M in 1991 to 3,45M in 2025, reaching a population density of 795,24 persons per km² (Table \ref{tab:density-post-soviet}). Neighbouring Fergana Region expanded from 2,23M to 4,11M across 7.113 km², attaining 577,64 persons per km², while Namangan Region climbed from 1,52M to 3,12M across 7.492 km², reaching 416,80 persons per km².

Collectively, the three Uzbek regions of the Fergana Valley housed 10,68M residents on just 18.945 km² in 2025, creating one of the densest agrarian-industrial rural settlement landscapes in the world [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Petrick2021Post; @Golunov2025Central]. High rural population densities placed severe demands on land, irrigation water from the Syr Darya and Naryn rivers and local employment opportunities, stimulating intensive internal migration toward Tashkent and seasonal labour migration toward the Russian Federation [@Kurbanova2022Impact; @Somerlikova2025Causes; @Petrick2021Post].

Across central and southern Uzbekistan, demographic expansion was similarly vigorous [@Kurbanova2024Demographi]. Samarkand Region grew from 2,23M in 1991 to 4,27M in 2025, Qashqadaryo climbed from 1,67M to 3,62M and Surxondaryo expanded from 1,32M to 2,96M [@Kurbanova2024Demographi]. Tashkent City grew from 2,13M to 3,12M, while the surrounding Tashkent Region expanded in tandem from 2,23M to 3,12M, creating an integrated urban-industrial agglomeration of over 6,24M inhabitants [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting]. In the west, the autonomous Republic of Karakalpakstan, despite severe environmental desiccation associated with the Aral Sea disaster, expanded from 1,26M to 2,05M, reflecting high marital fertility that offset acute ecological and public health challenges [@Mukhamejan2026Long; @Kurbanova2024Demographi].

```{r tab-regions, results='asis'}
yr_cols <- c("1991", "1995", "2000", "2005", "2010", "2015", "2020", "2025")

reg_rows <- lapply(names(mod_data$regions), function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) viscount_fmt_pop(rv$population[[y]]), character(1))
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  df_r <- data.frame(
    Region = nm,
    Area = viscount_fmt_number(rv$area_km2, 0L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
  for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
    df_r[[yr_cols[idx]]] <- vals[idx]
  }
  df_r
})
reg_df <- do.call(rbind, reg_rows)

tot_vals <- vapply(yr_cols, function(y) {
  tot <- sum(vapply(mod_data$regions, function(r) as.numeric(r$population[[y]]), numeric(1)))
  viscount_fmt_pop(tot)
}, character(1))

tot_row <- data.frame(
  Region = "Domain Total",
  Area = viscount_fmt_number(mod_data$total_area_km2, 0L),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
for (idx in seq_along(yr_cols)) {
  tot_row[[yr_cols[idx]]] <- tot_vals[idx]
}
reg_df <- rbind(reg_df, tot_row)
rownames(reg_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  reg_df,
  "Territorial population benchmarks across 48 administrative divisions of post-Soviet Central Asia, 1991 to 2025, calculated from regional registers.",
  c("Administrative Division", "Area (km²)", yr_cols),
  list(label = "tab:regions-post-soviet", font_size = "tiny", max_rows_per_page = 26L)
)
```

## Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan: Mountain Demography, Civil Strife and Labour Migration

The mountainous republics of Tajikistan and Kyrgyzstan followed distinctive demographic paths shaped by high elevation, limited arable valley floor and deep dependence on international labour remittances [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes; @Group2021Demographi].

In Tajikistan, the population nearly doubled over the study period, rising from 5,26M in 1991 to 10,44M in 2025 (+98,3%), the highest proportional expansion of any Central Asian republic (Table \ref{tab:validation-post-soviet}) [@OBrien2019Long; @Kurbanova2024Demographi]. The southern agricultural region of Khatlon expanded from 1,77M in 1991 to 3,70M in 2025, Sughd in the north grew from 1,57M to 2,96M and the Districts of Republican Subordination increased from 1,16M to 2,30M [@OBrien2019Long]. Dushanbe doubled from 607k to 1,23M, reflecting intense post-war centralization [@OBrien2019Long; @Group2021Demographi]. Only the high-altitude Pamir region of Gorno-Badakhshan remained sparsely populated, growing modestly from 152k to 247k across 57.650 km² (4,28 persons per km²) [@OBrien2019Long].

The rapid demographic expansion of Tajikistan occurred alongside massive outward labour mobility [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes; @Massey2023Shape]. Following the end of the Civil War in 1997, hundreds of thousands of Tajik workers entered the Russian labour market [@OBrien2019Long; @Hameed2023Analyzing]. By 2015, over one million Tajik citizens were estimated to be working in Russia at any given time, sending remittances that sustained rural households, financed residential construction and maintained local retail commerce [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. This migration stream produced significant demographic distortions in rural communities, characterized by male absentee rates exceeding 30% to 40% among cohorts aged 20 to 45, elevating female household headship and child-rearing responsibilities [@OBrien2019Long; @Kurbanova2022Impact].

Kyrgyzstan expanded from 4,35M in 1991 to 7,15M in 2025 (+64,3%) (Table \ref{tab:validation-post-soviet}) [@Group2021Demographi; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. The republic exhibits a clear north-south demographic polarity [@Group2021Demographi]. The southern oblasts of Osh and Jalal-Abad, located in the fertile Fergana basin, expanded vigorously: Osh Region and City climbed from 961k in 1991 to 1,89M in 2025 (64,62 persons per km²), while Jalal-Abad grew from 759k to 1,31M (38,54 persons per km²) [@Group2021Demographi]. Together with Batken (growing from 304k to 575k), southern Kyrgyzstan accounted for over 52,9% of the national population by 2025.

In the north, Bishkek City nearly doubled from 658k to 1,15M, absorbing hundreds of thousands of internal migrants from montane rural oblasts such as Naryn (growing slowly from 253k to 329k across 44.745 km²) and Talas (climbing from 202k to 247k) [@Group2021Demographi; @Cividino2020Revisiting]. In Chuy Region, initial Slavic emigration during the 1990s depressed population before peri-urban expansion around Bishkek lifted the total to 1,07M in 2025 [@Sushchiy2021Russian; @Group2021Demographi]. Issyk-Kul grew moderately from 405k to 575k [@Group2021Demographi].

```{r tab-density, results='asis'}
reg_keys <- names(mod_data$regions)
dens_rows <- lapply(reg_keys, function(rk) {
  rv <- mod_data$regions[[rk]]
  ar <- as.numeric(rv$area_km2)
  nm <- gsub("&", "and", rv$name, fixed = TRUE)
  n_sites <- sum(vapply(sett_data, function(s) identical(s$region_id, rk), logical(1)))
  p1991 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["1991"]])
  p2025 <- as.numeric(rv$population[["2025"]])
  data.frame(
    Division = nm,
    Settlements = viscount_fmt_number(n_sites, 0L),
    P1991 = viscount_fmt_pop(p1991),
    Dens1991 = viscount_fmt_number(p1991 / ar, 2L),
    P2025 = viscount_fmt_pop(p2025),
    Dens2025 = viscount_fmt_number(p2025 / ar, 2L),
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
})
dens_df <- do.call(rbind, dens_rows)
rownames(dens_df) <- NULL

viscount_table(
  dens_df,
  "Catalogued settlements, 1991 and 2025 population benchmarks and territorial densities (persons per km²) across 48 administrative divisions.",
  c("Administrative Division", "Settlements", "1991 Pop", "1991 (km²)", "2025 Pop", "2025 (km²)"),
  list(label = "tab:density-post-soviet", font_size = "tiny", max_rows_per_page = 26L)
)
```

## Turkmenistan: Desert Oasis Demography and Census Anomalies

Turkmenistan presents a unique demographic profile dominated by the hyper-arid Karakum Desert, which occupies over 80% of the national territory [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main]. Settlement is strictly confined to narrow linear oases fed by the Amu Darya, the Karakum Canal and mountain runoff from the Kopet Dag range [@Petrick2021Post; @Golunov2025Central].

Total population expanded from 3,79M in 1991 to 7,40M in 2025 (+94,9%) (Table \ref{tab:validation-post-soviet}) [@Group2021Demographi]. Ahal Region, which encompasses the national capital Ashgabat, expanded from 1,06M in 1991 to 2,05M in 2025, concentrating 27,8% of the national population [@Group2021Demographi]. In the east, Mary Region along the Murghab River grew from 860k to 1,64M, while Lebap Region along the middle Amu Darya expanded from 759k to 1,56M [@Group2021Demographi]. In the north, Dashoguz Region in the lower Amu Darya delta climbed from 708k to 1,56M [@Group2021Demographi]. In contrast, Balkan Region in the arid Caspian west grew modestly from 405k to 575k across 118.642 km² (4,85 persons per km²), anchored by oil and gas extraction in Balkanabat and Turkmenbashi [@Group2021Demographi].

Demographic analysis of Turkmenistan is complicated by official census practices [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main]. While the 1995 census published comprehensive figures recording 4,48M inhabitants, results from the December 2012 census were withheld from detailed public release and provisional figures from the December 2022 census reporting 7,06M have been questioned by international demographers who point to significant outward emigration to Turkey, Russia and Europe [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. The 7,40M figure for 2025 calibrated in this study reflects official administrative registers while incorporating spatial adjustments that reconcile urban housing construction, infrastructure expansion and vital event recordings [@Group2021Demographi].

# Analytical Caveats and Demographic Uncertainties

Three substantial demographic and methodological caveats condition precision in this post-Soviet synthesis [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @OBrien2019Long; @Group2021Demographi].

First, discrepancies between *de jure* (permanently registered) and *de facto* (physically present) population counts constitute an unavoidable challenge in high-migration settings [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. In Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, national censuses traditionally enumerate citizens registered in household propiska records, even if individuals have resided abroad as labour migrants for several consecutive years [@OBrien2019Long; @Group2021Demographi]. Independent household surveys suggest that at any benchmark year between 2005 and 2022, between 12% and 20% of adult males from Tajikistan and southern Kyrgyzstan were physically absent from their domestic enumeration districts [@OBrien2019Long; @Somerlikova2025Causes]. Consequently, official territorial population totals reflect registered legal populations rather than daily resident counts.

Second, the quality and transparency of census enumerations varied significantly across the five republics [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main]. While Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan conducted regular ten-year census rounds (1999, 2009, 2021-2022) with published microdata and international methodological observation, Uzbekistan did not conduct a comprehensive post-Soviet population census between 1989 and 2025, relying instead on continuous administrative registers maintained by local self-governing community bodies (*mahallas*) and civil registration bureaus [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Group2021Demographi]. While Uzbekistan's administrative registration system captures births and deaths with high precision, inter-provincial migration tracking remains subject to registration delays [@Kurbanova2024Demographi; @Group2021Demographi]. In Turkmenistan, official statistical reticence necessitates careful spatial modelling to cross-validate published velayat aggregates [@Group2021Demographi; @Sheriyazdanov2025Main].

Third, internal unregistered peri-urban informal settlements create micro-spatial enumeration disparities around major metropolises [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Cividino2020Revisiting; @Group2021Demographi]. Rapid internal migration toward Bishkek, Almaty, Shymkent and Tashkent produced extensive peri-urban residential belts (*novostroiki* and dacha communities) that frequently lacked formal municipal registration, leading to temporary under-counting in official city statistics and corresponding over-counting in rural origin districts [@Aubakirova2024Regional; @Cividino2020Revisiting]. The settlement register harmonised in this study accounts for these suburban agglomerations by defining metropolitan settlement clusters around major urban nodes [@Cividino2020Revisiting].
